Monte Carlo Simulation and the Bootstrap

A simulation answers a model's question with an error that the draws measure themselves: how many draws an answer needs, how to need fewer, and what resampling the days keeps and destroys.

Volume III · ProbabilityBuilds on LM1 · LM2 · LM5 · LM12 · LM13 · LM14 · LM15 · LM16 · LM17Leads to LM19 · LM20 · LM22 · LM26 · LM30 · LM32 · LM34 · LM36 · LM38 · LM39 · LM45Time ≈ 3 h + labPDF A4 print edition
Learning Outcomes
MasteryAfter this module you should be able to:
1explain how a seeded generator makes a simulation reproducible, and bump and reprice with common random numbers
2draw from the exponential, normal and empirical distributions by the inverse transform, and normal vectors by colouring
3calculate a Monte Carlo estimate, its standard error and its 95% Monte Carlo interval, and explain the 1/n​ rate
4compare Monte Carlo integration with Simpson's rule, and explain why simulation wins in many dimensions
5apply antithetic variates, control variates and importance sampling, and predict each one's variance reduction
6apply the iid bootstrap to a mean and a five-year growth factor, and explain what resampling days keeps and destroys
7implement reproducible simulations and bootstraps with NumPy's Generator and SciPy, in chunks
Learning Module Overview
  • Of TR23's 4,619 overlapping five-year windows of 1,231 sessions, 191 ended below their start (4.1%), all from two episodes. A model of iid normal daily log returns answers 5.49% by a formula; a Monte Carlo simulation of it answers 5.3% and an iid bootstrap of the days 5.6%, each ± 0.2 points with 10,000 draws.
  • A seeded generator is a deterministic recursion. default_rng([1, 20261011]) gives 249 draws at or below −2 in 10,000 on every rerun, and another stream gives 214, against 227.5 expected: a rerun reproduces, only a new stream replicates.
  • The inverse transform FY−1​(U) turns uniform draws into any distribution: exponential waits −ln(1−U)/λ, normal draws Φ−1(U) and TAIEX days R(⌈uT⌉)​; colouring gives normal vectors LZ.
  • A Monte Carlo mean has standard error sY​/n​, so ten times the accuracy costs a hundred times the draws. The rate explains LM12's colouring gap of 0.0250: for 4,382 draws the root-mean-square gap is 0.0289.
  • On LM5's −5% tail, Simpson's rule reaches a relative error of 1.23×10−6 with 257 evaluations, where plain Monte Carlo would need about 3.3×1016 draws. In N dimensions a grid errs by O(n−4/N) and Monte Carlo by O(n−1/2).
  • Importance sampling divides the variance of that tail estimate by 10,786. Antithetic paths divide the variance of the five-year mean by 6.06 and a control variate by 11.4, while antithetics gain nothing on a tail probability.
  • The iid bootstrap draws days from the empirical distribution. Its mean of T days has variance s2/T, and its growth factor over m days has mean (1+Rˉ)m=2.1580, both exactly.
  • Resampling keeps the one-day law, 7 April 2025 included, and destroys the clustering: the monthly count of days with ∣R∣≥3% has variance 1.846 in the data and 0.598 in resamples.

1Introduction

Volume III has built probability models for TAIEX's returns (LM13 to LM17), and many questions about such a model have no formula. A Monte Carlo simulation answers them by drawing from the model many times. The bootstrap draws instead from the data's own empirical distribution. Both answers carry an error that the draws themselves measure.

Motivating CaseUnder water after five years?

TR23 is the TAIEX total-return index, dividends reinvested: 5,849 daily returns from 3 January 2003 to 8 October 2026. Five years is 1,231 sessions. Of the 4,619 five-year windows that start on a close in the sample, 191 ended below their start: 4.1%. All 191 started between November 2003 and April 2004 or between June and December 2007 (Exhibit 1). So they record two episodes, and the sample holds fewer than five non-overlapping five-year periods.

A model of independent, normal daily log returns fitted to TR23 answers 5.49% by a formula. A Monte Carlo simulation of that model answers 5.3% (Example 3), and an iid bootstrap of the days 5.6% (Example 10), each ± 0.2 points with 10,000 draws. How far can each answer be trusted, and what does each one assume?

Sections 2 and 3 draw random numbers from any distribution. Section 4 measures simulation error, and Section 5 compares simulation with numerical integration. Section 6 shrinks the error, Section 7 resamples the days, and Section 8 collects the Python.

NoteNotation for this module

The sample is TR23: closes 2 January 2003 → 8 October 2026, T=5,849 daily returns Rt​ from 3 January 2003, log returns rt​=ln(1+Rt​), 23.7645 years, A=246.12. Moments divide by T: Rˉ=0.062505%, s=1.2084%, rˉ=0.05517% and sr​=1.2107%. Five years is m=round(5A)=1,231 sessions. Quantiles are order statistics R(⌈uT⌉)​ (LM14).

Local symbols: Y a simulated quantity with n independent draws Yi​, their mean Yˉn​, standard deviation σY​ in the model and sY​ over the draws (divisor n); Y=h(Z); p the probability an indicator estimates, p^​ its estimate; Yi−​ the antithetic partner (not Y~i​, which recalls LM12's centred X~), ρ−​ the pair's correlation; X a control with known mean μX​, β=σXY​/σX2​, β^​ its estimate; a a shift and −k a threshold (no bets here); λ an exponential rate per session; L a Cholesky factor (no leverage); N a dimension; B the number of resamples (no Brownian motion); EF^​, VarF^​, PrF^​ for days drawn from F^; Rˉboot​ and Gboot​ a resample's mean of T days and growth factor over m days (no star, which marks an optimum); Σ^sim​ a simulated covariance matrix, ∥M∥F​ the Frobenius norm. Indices: i draws, t days, j ranks.

NoteResearch hygiene

Every model of TAIEX here is fitted to all of TR23, so its answers are in-sample, not forecasts. The windows and monthly counts are descriptive. A 95% Monte Carlo interval measures simulation error only, never model error. Resampling ignores the order of days, so a bootstrap is no test on later data (LM22 resamples blocks; LM34 tests on later data).

2Pseudo-Random Numbers and Seeds

explain how a seeded generator makes a simulation reproducible, and bump and reprice with common random numbers

A computer draws random numbers by arithmetic.

Example 1Same seed, same answer

Count the draws at or below −2 among 10,000 standard normal draws from default_rng([1, 20261011]). Run it twice, then once more with default_rng([16, 20261011]).

Solution

The first run gives 249 hits, and the rerun gives 249 again, draw for draw. The second stream gives 214. Since Φ(−2)=0.02275, the model expects 227.5 hits, and a binomial count has standard deviation np(1−p)​=14.9 by (15.2). Both counts lie within 1.5 standard deviations of 227.5. A rerun reproduces a number; only a new stream replicates the experiment.

The generator

A pseudo-random number generator is a deterministic recursion. A seed sets its internal state, and each step updates the state and outputs a number. NumPy's default_rng(seed) builds a Generator on the PCG64 algorithm, whose sequence repeats only after 2128 steps (O'Neill 2014; stated without proof).

The Generator turns the outputs into uniform draws on [0,1). A random variable U is uniform, U∼Unif(0,1), when Pr(U≤u)=u for 0≤u≤1. The draws are designed to behave like iid uniform draws, independent as in (16.1). This book does not test generators.

One stream per experiment

Every simulated experiment in this module creates its generator once, at its start, as default_rng([e, 20261011]), with e the experiment's number. Example 4 alone keeps LM12's seed, because it re-runs that lab. Each experiment has its own generator, so resizing one leaves the others unchanged. Through NumPy's SeedSequence, different values of e give streams that are independent with very high probability. A generator reseeded inside a loop would repeat its draws.

Rerunning with the same seed reproduces a result exactly, which checks the code, not the estimate. Running with another seed replicates the experiment, and the spread of the replications shows the simulation error. NumPy promises identical streams only for the same version and build, so the printed numbers rest on the NumPy that uv.lock pins.

PitfallBump and reprice with common random numbers

Bumping and repricing a Monte Carlo value with LM2's central difference (2.11) divides the difference of two simulations by a small step, which magnifies their errors. With common random numbers, both runs use the same draws, so most of their errors cancel. For the slope of Pr(Z≤−k) at k=2 with Δk=0.01 and 100,000 draws a side, the standard error falls from 0.0333 to 0.0052 (Problem 11).

導讀隨機種子：重現不等於重複實驗

電腦產生的隨機數（random number）其實是擬隨機數（pseudo-random number）：擬隨機數產生器（pseudo-random number generator）是確定的遞迴（recursion），隨機種子（random seed）決定起始狀態，之後每一步都算得出來。它的輸出設計成像獨立同分布（iid）的均勻分布（uniform distribution）抽樣，這正是蒙地卡羅法（Monte Carlo method）需要的模型。同一個種子重跑一次，每個數字都一模一樣，只證明程式沒變，不是第二次檢驗；換一個種子才是重複實驗，結果之間的差距就是模擬誤差。本模組每個實驗（重跑 LM12 的 Example 4 除外）在開頭建立一次自己的產生器 default_rng([e, 20261011])，之後不再重設。用中央差分（central difference）估計導數（derivative）時，兩邊的計算要共用同一組隨機數（common random numbers），誤差才會大部分抵銷。

Knowledge Check 1

A colleague reruns your simulation with the same seed and gets the same estimate. Is that a second check of the estimate?

Answer

No. The same seed repeats every draw, so the rerun checks the code, not the simulation error. A new stream replicates the experiment, and the gap between 249 and 214 hits in Example 1 shows the error.

3From Uniform Draws to Any Distribution

draw from the exponential, normal and empirical distributions by the inverse transform, and normal vectors by colouring

A uniform draw u can be read as a probability level. In Exhibit 2, mark u on the vertical axis of TR23's empirical distribution function F^, (13.12), move right to the first step that reaches u, and read the return below. That return is the empirical quantile F^−1(u)=R(⌈uT⌉)​ of LM14.

TheoremInverse transform

Let U∼Unif(0,1), and let FY​ be a distribution function with LM14's quantile function FY−1​(u)=min{y:FY​(y)≥u} for 0<u<1. Then

Pr(FY−1​(U)≤y)=FY​(y)for every y,(18.1)
so FY−1​(U) has distribution function FY​.

When FY​ is continuous and strictly increasing, FY−1​ is its ordinary inverse and is increasing. So FY−1​(U)≤y exactly when U≤FY​(y), an event of probability FY​(y) (Grinstead and Snell 1997, §5.2, Corollary 5.2). Deep Dive (a) proves the general case (Glasserman 2003, §2.2.1).

Deep Dive(a) Proof of (18.1) for any distribution functionoptional · click to expand

Here FY​ is any distribution function: non-decreasing, right-continuous, with limits 0 and 1 (LM13). Fix u in (0,1). The set {y:FY​(y)≥u} is not empty, because FY​→1, and bounded below, because FY​→0. Right-continuity carries FY​≥u from the set to its infimum, so the infimum is a minimum and FY​(FY−1​(u))≥u.

Now FY−1​(u)≤y if and only if u≤FY​(y). If u≤FY​(y), then y lies in the set, so the minimum is at most y. If FY−1​(u)≤y, then FY​(y)≥FY​(FY−1​(u))≥u, since FY​ is non-decreasing. Hence Pr(FY−1​(U)≤y)=Pr(U≤FY​(y))=FY​(y). ■

The exponential distribution. A waiting time Y≥0 with FY​(y)=1−e−λy follows Exp(λ), with rate λ>0. Solving u=1−e−λy gives FY−1​(u)=−ln(1−u)/λ. Its mean is 1/λ (integrate by parts, LM5), and its median is ln2/λ, the y with FY​(y)=1/2.

Normal draws. For the standard normal, Φ−1(U)∼N(0,1), and μ+σΦ−1(U)∼N(μ,σ2) by (15.6).

Days from F^. The rank ⌈uT⌉ equals j exactly when (j−1)/T<u≤j/T, an interval of length 1/T. So the inverse transform on F^ draws each of the T days with probability 1/T: it picks a day uniformly at random.

Example 2A waiting time and a TAIEX day from three uniforms

Experiment 2's generator default_rng([2, 20261011]) gives random(3) = 0.1396965, 0.4634985 and 0.1740834 (seven decimals). Turn them into waiting times between days with ∣R∣≥3% under an exponential model, and into TAIEX days drawn from F^.

Solution

TR23 has 175 days with ∣R∣≥3% (LM14), so the model's rate is λ=175/5,849=0.02992 per session. The waits −ln(1−u)/λ are 5.03, 20.81 and 6.39 sessions. The model's mean wait is 1/λ=33.42 sessions and its median ln2/λ=23.17.

For F^, the ranks ⌈5,849u⌉ are 818, 2,712 and 1,019; seven decimals matter, since 5,849×0.4634985=2,711.003. The draws are R(818)​=−0.9468% (2021-12-14), R(2712)​=+0.0247% (2007-02-01) and R(1019)​=−0.7785% (2005-09-23), the points of Exhibit 2. The waits are model values, while the three returns are real days.

Normal vectors. For N independent standard normal draws Z and LL⊤=Σ, (16.7) gives LZ∼NN​(0,Σ), the colouring of LM12 (Glasserman 2003, §2.3.3). Section 4 measures how close a coloured sample comes to Σ.

PitfallA uniform draw can be 0

Generator.random returns numbers in [0,1), and 0 is possible. Then −lnU is infinite and ⌈TU⌉=0 is no rank, while 1−U lies in (0,1]. Draw waits as −ln(1−U)/λ, and draw ranks with integers(0, T), which returns the indices 0 to T−1 directly.

導讀逆變換法：把機率水準換成數值

逆變換法（inverse transform）把均勻分布（uniform distribution）的抽樣 u 當成機率水準，再用分位數函數（quantile function）換成任何分布的抽樣：FY−1​(U) 的累積分布函數（distribution function）就是 FY​。指數分布（exponential distribution）的等待時間（waiting time）是 −ln(1−U)/λ，常態分布（normal distribution）的抽樣是 Φ−1(U)，多變量常態分布（multivariate normal distribution）的向量則用 L 著色（colouring）。對經驗分布函數（empirical distribution function）F^ 做逆變換，等於從 5,849 個交易日中等機率挑一天，這是第 7 節自助重抽法（bootstrap）的基礎。random 可能剛好抽到 0，所以等待時間要用 −ln(1−U)/λ，排名則直接用 integers 抽。

Knowledge Check 2

Why is −lnU/λ also an Exp(λ) draw, and which return does u=0.5 draw from F^?

Answer

If U is uniform, so is 1−U, so −lnU/λ has the law of −ln(1−U)/λ; only U=0 must be avoided. For u=0.5 the rank is ⌈2,924.5⌉=2,925, and R(2925)​=+0.0879% is TR23's median (LM14).

4The Monte Carlo Estimator and Its Error

calculate a Monte Carlo estimate, its standard error and its 95% Monte Carlo interval, and explain the 1/n​ rate

Every answer the case asks for is an expectation: a probability is E[1A​] by (14.1), and the mean growth factor is EG. For a standard normal Z, Eh(Z)=∫h(z)φ(z)dz by (5.9), and a path of m days is an integral in m dimensions. The Monte Carlo estimator replaces the integral by the average of n independent draws.

TheoremThe Monte Carlo estimator

Let Y1​,…,Yn​ be iid draws of Y with E∣Y∣<∞, and Yˉn​=n1​∑i​Yi​. Then EYˉn​=EY, and Yˉn​→EY with probability one as n→∞. If also σY2​<∞,

VarYˉn​=nσY2​​,standard error n​sY​​.(18.2)

The mean and the variance are (17.1), and the convergence is the strong law of LM17 (Durrett 2019, Theorem 2.4.1). The standard error sY​/n​ estimates the standard deviation of Yˉn​ from the draws themselves. It shrinks like 1/n​, so ten times the accuracy costs a hundred times the draws.

By the central limit theorem (17.5), Yˉn​ is close to normal for large n, so it lies within 1.96σY​/n​ of EY with probability close to 0.95. With sY​ for σY​, this gives the 95% Monte Carlo interval

Yˉn​±1.96n​sY​​,0<σY2​<∞, n large.(18.3)

The interval (18.3) misses EY in about one run in twenty. It is approximate: close with thousands of draws, but not when the draws contain few hits of a rare event (Section 5). LM20 develops standard errors and confidence intervals for data. A printed estimate keeps only the digits its standard error supports: 0.0530±0.0022 prints as 5.3% ± 0.2 points.

Other standard errors. An indicator Y=1A​ has Y2=Y, so σY2​=p(1−p) and the standard error is p^​(1−p^​)/n​. For near-normal draws, sY2​ has relative standard error about 2/n​ by Var(Z2)=2, (14.6). A square root halves a small relative error (LM2's tangent line), so sY​ has standard error about sY​/2n​.

For a quantile or a slope, compute the statistic on 20 equal batches of the draws. For large n its variance falls about like 1/n, as (17.1) gives for a mean (stated without proof; Glasserman 2003, §9.1.2, for a quantile; LM23 for a slope). So a batch 20 times smaller gives about 20 times the variance, and the standard deviation of the 20 values (divisor 20) over 20​ approximates the standard error.

Example 3The case by simulation

In the case's model, daily log returns are iid N(g,σr2​) with g=rˉ=0.05517% and σr​=sr​=1.2107%. Find Pr(G<1) for m=1,231 sessions exactly, then from 10,000 paths simulated with default_rng([3, 20261011]).

Solution

By (1.12), lnG=∑t​rt​ is a sum of m iid normal log returns, so lnG∼N(mg,mσr2​) by (16.7), and (17.6) holds exactly. Hence Pr(G<1)=Φ(−gm​/σr​)=Φ(−1.5988)=5.49%.

Experiment 3 draws standard_normal((500, m)) twenty times and sums g+σr​Zt​ along each row. Of the 10,000 paths, 530 end under water, so p^​=0.0530 with standard error 0.0530×0.9470/10,000​=0.0022. The 95% Monte Carlo interval, about 4.9% to 5.7%, covers 5.49%, and the simulation reports 5.3% ± 0.2 points.

Why LM12's colouring gap was 0.0250

LM12's lab coloured 4,382 standard normal vectors with S5's Cholesky factor. Their covariance matrix missed Σ by a relative 0.0250, and the lab left the rate to this module. Let X1​,…,Xn​ be iid NN​(0,Σ), and let Σ^sim​=n1​∑i​Xi​Xi⊤​. Measure the gap with the Frobenius norm ∥M∥F​, the square root of the sum of the squared entries. Deep Dive (b) proves

E∥Σ^sim​−Σ∥F2​=n∥Σ∥F2​+(trΣ)2​.(18.4)

The root-mean-square relative gap is therefore

∥Σ∥F​(E∥Σ^sim​−Σ∥F2​)1/2​=n1+(trΣ)2/∥Σ∥F2​​​,

a 1/n​ rate again.

Example 4Was a gap of 0.0250 large?

LM12's lab drew standard_normal((4382, 5)) from default_rng(20261011), coloured the rows with S5's factor L and compared np.cov(..., ddof=0) of the result with Σ=LL⊤. Here its 4,382 draws are n.

Solution

The same draws, coloured with LM12's printed L, give the gap 0.0250. Semiconductor's simulated variance, for example, is 4.18% too high, about two standard errors of 2/n​=2/4,382​=2.14%, since Var(Z2)=2.

For S5, (trΣ)2/∥Σ∥F2​=2.6509, so the root-mean-square relative gap is 1.911/n​: 0.0289 at n=4,382 and 0.0085 at 50,000. In Exhibit 3, 82 of 200 runs (41%) come at or below 0.0250, so LM12's run was ordinary.

Deep Dive(b) Proof of (18.4)optional · click to expand

Let X1​ and X2​ be two entries of X∼NN​(0,Σ), bivariate normal by (16.7), with standard deviations σ1​, σ2​ and correlation ρ12​. The matching entries of Σ are σ11​=σ12​, σ22​=σ22​ and σ12​=ρ12​σ1​σ2​. Colour them with their own 2×2 factor, for independent standard normal Z1​ and Z2​:

X1​=σ1​Z1​,X2​=σ2​(ρ12​Z1​+1−ρ122​​Z2​).​
Then X1​X2​=σ1​σ2​(ρ12​Z12​+1−ρ122​​Z1​Z2​), and the two terms are uncorrelated because E[Z13​Z2​]=0. With Var(Z12​)=2 from (14.6) and Var(Z1​Z2​)=1,
Var(X1​X2​)​=σ11​σ22​(2ρ122​+1−ρ122​)=σ11​σ22​+σ122​.​
The same steps give Var(X12​)=2σ112​, the formula with both entries equal. Each entry of Σ^sim​ is a mean of n iid copies of such a product, and its mean is the matching entry of Σ. By (17.1) its expected squared error is the product's variance over n.

Summing over all N2 positions of Σ, the terms σ11​σ22​ add up to (trΣ)2 and the terms σ122​ to ∥Σ∥F2​, which is (18.4). The call np.cov(..., ddof=0) centres the draws first, which changes the root-mean-square gap by under 0.4% for S5 when n≥100. ■

PitfallThe interval measures simulation error only

The interval of Example 3 says that more paths would bring the estimate close to 5.49%, the model's own answer. It says nothing about TAIEX, because the model assumes independent normal days fitted to the whole sample. The formula is exact under the model; every simulated number only approximates it.

導讀蒙地卡羅估計：誤差以 1/n​ 的速度縮小

蒙地卡羅法（Monte Carlo method）把期望值（expectation）寫成積分（integral），再用 n 個獨立同分布（iid）抽樣的平均去估計它。強大數法則（strong law of large numbers）保證平均會收斂，標準誤（standard error）sY​/n​ 則告訴我們誤差有多大：精確度要提高 10 倍，抽樣數就得增加 100 倍。由中央極限定理（central limit theorem），「估計值 ± 1.96 個標準誤」是 95% Monte Carlo interval，也就是只量模擬誤差的區間，不是對台股的信賴區間（confidence interval）。印出的位數要配合標準誤：0.0530±0.0022 只能寫成 5.3% ± 0.2 個百分點。下一節會看到，這個速度與維度無關，所以高維度時模擬通常比格點上的數值積分（quadrature）有效率，只是單次抽樣的標準差（standard deviation）σY​ 可能隨維度變大。

Knowledge Check 3

How many paths of Example 3 would bring the standard error of Pr(G<1) down to 0.1 point?

Answer

The standard error is p(1−p)/n​, so n=p(1−p)/0.0012=0.0549×0.9451/10−6, about 52,000 paths, five times as many as Example 3 used.

5Monte Carlo Against Quadrature

compare Monte Carlo integration with Simpson's rule, and explain why simulation wins in many dimensions

LM5 computed a normal tail probability by numerical integration, or quadrature. Compare it with simulation.

Example 5Against Simpson's rule

LM5's normal model gave 0050 a −5% day with probability p=Pr(Z≤−4.1074386)=2.000355×10−5, which LM5 approximated by Simpson's rule. Estimate p from 106 plain Monte Carlo draws of default_rng([5, 20261011]), and compare the costs.

Solution

Experiment 5 draws standard_normal(10**6): 18 draws fall at or below −4.1074386, against 20.0 expected, so the estimate is 1.8×10−5±0.4×10−5. Its 95% Monte Carlo interval covers p. Per draw the relative standard error is (1−p)/p​=223.6, so with 106 draws it is 22%.

A 95% Monte Carlo interval of ±1% needs (1.96/0.01)2(1−p)/p=1.92×109 draws. Simpson's rule reached a relative error of 1.23×10−6 with 257 evaluations of φ (LM5). Plain Monte Carlo would need about 3.3×1016 draws for that relative standard error. Exhibit 4 plots both rates against the evaluations.

Simulation wins in many dimensions. On a product grid, Simpson's rule errs by O(Δx4) in each coordinate of a smooth integrand, by (5.14) one coordinate at a time. With equal points on each of N axes, n evaluations give a spacing of order n−1/N, so the error is O(n−4/N). Monte Carlo's standard error is σY​/n​ in any dimension, though σY​ may grow with N.

The case is an integral over m=1,231 coordinates. A grid with two points per axis would need 21231 evaluations, a number of 371 digits, while Example 3 needed 10,000 paths. Quasi-Monte Carlo methods, which use evenly spread points, are not in this book.

PitfallZero hits report 0±0

With 10,000 plain draws at k=4.1074386, the expected number of hits is 0.2, and no hit occurs with probability (1−p)10000=0.8187. In 82% of such runs the estimate and its standard error are both 0, and the interval 0±0 excludes the true value. The interval (18.3) needs enough hits to estimate σY​, so count them first.

Knowledge Check 4

What is the chance that 105 plain draws produce no hit at or below −4.1074386?

Answer

The chance is (1−p)100000=0.135, close to e−2 since the expected number of hits is 2.0. About one run in seven reports 0±0.

6Variance Reduction

apply antithetic variates, control variates and importance sampling, and predict each one's variance reduction

Exhibit 5 shows three ways to get a smaller error from the same number of draws. Each changes what is averaged, keeps its expectation and lowers its variance.

Antithetic variates

Since −Z has the same law as Z, the partner Yi−​=h(−Zi​) of Yi​=h(Zi​) has the same law as Yi​. Average each pair. By (16.3), Var(21​(Yi​+Yi−​))=41​σY2​(2+2ρ−​), so for n pairs, independent across i, and σY2​<∞,

Var(n1​i=1∑n​21​(Yi​+Yi−​))=2nσY2​​(1+ρ−​).​(18.5)

Plain sampling with the same 2n evaluations has variance σY2​/(2n). So antithetic pairs multiply the variance by 1+ρ−​, and they help only when ρ−​<0. When Y=h(Z) with h non-decreasing in every coordinate (or non-increasing in every one), ρ−​≤0 (stated without proof; Glasserman 2003, §4.2, p. 207).

Example 6Antithetic paths

Estimate the model's five-year mean growth factor EG with 5,000 antithetic pairs from default_rng([6, 20261011]), and compare with the 10,000 plain paths of Example 3.

Solution

By (5.12), EG=em(g+σr2​/2)=2.1584. Experiment 6 draws standard_normal((500, m)) ten times, and builds a path from each row Z and its partner from −Z. The 5,000 pairs give 2.155±0.004, against 2.165±0.010 from the plain paths.

The partner of G is e2mg/G, and G increases in every Zt​. By Problem 5, ρ−​=−e−mσr2​=−0.835 with mσr2​=0.1804, so the variance falls by the factor 1/(1+ρ−​)=6.06. For Pr(G<1) the pairs give 0.0528±0.0022: a path and its partner cannot both end under water, so ρ−​=−p/(1−p)=−0.058 with p=0.0549, a factor of only 1.06.

Control variates

Suppose each draw also yields a quantity X whose mean μX​ is known exactly, such as lnG with mean mg. Then Y−β(X−μX​) has the mean of Y for every constant β. By (16.3) its variance is σY2​−2βσXY​+β2σX2​, smallest at β=σXY​/σX2​. Hence, for iid pairs (Xi​,Yi​) with finite variances, σX​>0 and known μX​,

Var(Yˉn​−β(Xˉn​−μX​))=n(1−ρXY2​)σY2​​atβ=σX2​σXY​​.​(18.6)

The best β is the least-squares slope of Y on X, so β^​ comes from the draws as in (12.3) of LM12. Estimating β from the same draws adds a bias, typically of order 1/n (stated without proof; Glasserman 2003, §4.1.3).

Example 7A control variate for the five-year mean

On the paths of Example 3, use X=lnG, whose mean mg=0.6791 is known, as a control for Y=G and for Y=1{G<1}.

Solution

The least-squares slope of G on lnG is β^​=2.18 (batch standard error 0.01). Exactly, β=EG=2.1584, because completing the square as in (5.12) gives Cov(G,lnG)=mσr2​EG. The controlled estimate is 2.161±0.003, against 2.165±0.010 plain.

The exact correlation of the control with Y=G is

ρXY​=(emσr2​−1mσr2​​)1/2=0.955,
and with the indicator Y=1{G<1} it is
ρXY​=−p(1−p)​φ(1.5988)​=−0.488.
The variance falls by the factor 1/(1−ρXY2​): 11.4 for G, but only 1.31 for the indicator, whose controlled estimate is 0.0535±0.0020.

Importance sampling

A tail event is rare under N(0,1) but common under a normal shifted towards it (Glasserman 2003, §4.6). Completing the square gives φ(z)eaz−a2/2=φ(z−a). Substituting x=z−a in (5.9) then gives, for every a and every h with E∣h(Z)∣<∞,

Eh(Z)=E[h(Z−a)eaZ−a2/2],Pr(Z≤−k)=E[1{Z≤0}ekZ−k2/2].​(18.7)

The second line takes a=k: the shifted draw Z−k lands in the tail about half the time, and the weight ekZ−k2/2 corrects for the shift. Deep Dive (c) gives the second moment of one draw, ek2Φ(−2k) at a=k. LM32 applies these estimators to value at risk.

Example 8Importance sampling for LM5's tail

Estimate p=Pr(Z≤−4.1074386) by (18.7) with a=k=4.1074386 from 10,000 draws of default_rng([8, 20261011]).

Solution

Experiment 8 draws standard_normal(10_000). Of the shifted draws Z−k, 5,043 land in the tail, and the weighted average is 2.047×10−5±0.044×10−5, a relative standard error of 2.1%. The exact 2.000355×10−5 lies inside its 95% Monte Carlo interval.

By Deep Dive (c), one draw has variance ek2Φ(−2k)−p2=1.8546×10−9, against p(1−p)=2.0003×10−5 for a plain draw. The ratio is 10,786, so these 10,000 draws do the work of 1.08×108 plain ones. Three significant digits would give 10,811.

Deep Dive(c) The second moment of importance samplingoptional · click to expand

One draw of (18.7) for h(z)=1{z≤−k} is Y=1{Z≤a−k}eaZ−a2/2, so Y2=1{Z≤a−k}e2aZ−a2. Completing the square, φ(z)e2az=e2a2φ(z−2a), so

E[Y2]​=ea2∫−∞a−k​φ(z−2a)dz=ea2Φ(−k−a).​
At a=k the second moment is ek2Φ(−2k), and the variance of one draw is ek2Φ(−2k)−p2. ■

PitfallA shift too far out

The relative standard error of one draw, ea2Φ(−k−a)−p2​/p, is 7.76 at a=k/2, 2.15 at a=k and 132 at a=2k, against 223.6 for a plain draw. Shifted too far, most draws land deep in the tail with tiny weights, and a rare draw near the threshold carries a huge one. The shifted law must also be positive wherever hφ=0, as a normal always is.

The widget runs the three estimators of Pr(Z≤−k) on one stream of draws.

導讀變異數縮減：同樣的抽樣數，更小的誤差

變異數縮減（variance reduction）不改變估計的期望值（expectation），只改變平均的對象。對偶變數（antithetic variates）把 Z 和 −Z 配成一對，相關係數（correlation coefficient）ρ−​ 為負時才有用：估計五年成長倍數（growth factor）的期望值時，估計值的變異數（variance）縮小 6.06 倍，但尾端機率的兩個事件（event）互斥（disjoint），幾乎沒有幫助。控制變量（control variate）利用期望值已知的 lnG，變異數乘上 1−ρXY2​，最適係數就是最小平方法（least squares）的斜率（slope）。重要抽樣（importance sampling）把抽樣用的常態分布（normal distribution）平移到尾端，再用權重（weight）修正：估計 LM5 的 −5% 尾端機率時，估計值的變異數縮小 10,786 倍。移得太遠反而更糟，靠近門檻的少數抽樣會帶著極大的權重。

Knowledge Check 5

Why do antithetic pairs not help with Pr(Z≤−k)?

Answer

The pair is 1{Z≤−k} and 1{Z≥k}, which cannot both be 1. So E[Yi​Yi−​]=0 and ρ−​=−p2/(p(1−p))=−p/(1−p), only −2.0×10−5 at k=4.1074386. The variance falls by the factor 1.00002: a pair costs two evaluations and is worth two plain draws, no more.

7The iid Bootstrap

apply the iid bootstrap to a mean and a five-year growth factor, and explain what resampling days keeps and destroys

The model of Sections 4–6 assumed normal days. The iid bootstrap instead takes the empirical distribution F^, mass 1/T on each of TR23's returns, as the model (Efron and Tibshirani 1993, ch. 6). A resample draws days with replacement, each with probability 1/T at every draw, and integers(0, T, size=T) gives the indices. By Section 3, a resample is a set of iid draws from F^, as in (13.13).

Under F^, a drawn day has mean T1​∑t​Rt​=Rˉ and variance T1​∑t​(Rt​−Rˉ)2=s2. A resample mean Rˉboot​ averages T such iid days, so (17.1) gives

EF^​Rˉboot​=Rˉ,VarF^​(Rˉboot​)=Ts2​.(18.8)

Both moments in (18.8) are exact properties of the bootstrap model. LM20 derives the same s/T​ as the sampling error of Rˉ.

Example 9The bootstrap of the mean day

With default_rng([9, 20261011]), draw B=10,000 resamples of 5,849 days, and compare the spread of their means with (18.8).

Solution

Experiment 9 draws integers(0, T, size=(500, T)) twenty times. The resample means average 0.06272%±0.00016%, against Rˉ=0.062505%, and their standard deviation (divisor B) is 0.01563%±0.00011%, with standard error sY​/2B​. By (18.8) the exact value is s/T​=1.2084%/5,849​=0.01580%, 1.5 standard errors away. Efron and Tibshirani's (6.6) divides by B−1, which changes nothing here. Wasserman (2004, §8.2) divides by B in his (8.1), as this module does.

The growth factor. A resample of m days has growth factor Gboot​, the product of 1+R over its drawn days. These days are independent with mean Rˉ, so (17.4) with μ=Rˉ gives

EF^​Gboot​=(1+Rˉ)m.(18.9)

The log of Gboot​ is a sum of m iid drawn log returns, with mean mrˉ and variance msr2​ exactly, the two moments of the normal model of Example 3. Over 1,231 days the central limit theorem then makes the shape of one day matter little, so the two models agree.

Example 10The case by bootstrap

With default_rng([10, 20261011]), draw B=10,000 resamples of m=1,231 days, and estimate PrF^​(Gboot​<1), EF^​Gboot​ and the quantiles of Gboot​.

Solution

Experiment 10 draws integers(0, T, size=(500, m)) twenty times. Of the 10,000 resamples, 561 end under water: 0.0561±0.0023, printed 5.6% ± 0.2 points.

By (18.9), EF^​Gboot​=1.000625051231=2.1580. The plain estimate 2.136±0.009 has the 95% Monte Carlo interval 2.118 to 2.154, which misses 2.1580, as one run in twenty does. With lnGboot​ as a control, whose mean mrˉ is exact, the estimate is 2.158±0.003.

The same draws put the average lnGboot​ 2.4 standard errors below mrˉ. Partly for this reason, the quantiles of Gboot​ at 5%, 50% and 95% sit slightly below the normal model's 0.98 / 1.97 / 3.97. They are 0.97 / 1.94 / 3.94, with batch standard errors 0.008, 0.010 and 0.034. The standard deviation of lnGboot​ is 0.424±0.003, against m​sr​=0.425 exactly.

Why the windows differ. The windows give a narrower spread of lnG, 0.283 against 0.425 (Exhibit 6). They overlap, so they record two episodes in fewer than five disjoint periods, and they weight days unequally: their mean lnG is 0.502, against mrˉ=0.679. Their error needs a bootstrap of blocks (LM22), and LM19 asks whether the spread grows like m​.

What resampling keeps and destroys

Every resampled day is one of TR23's days, so resampling keeps the one-day law exactly. The 15 days at or below −5% (LM13) recur at their own frequency, 7 April 2025 (−9.6997%) among them.

Resampling ignores the order of days, so it destroys their clustering. Exhibit 7 counts the days with ∣R∣≥3% in each calendar month. TR23 has three months with eight (September 2008, October 2008 and March 2020), and a monthly variance of 1.846 (LM15). Resamples placed on TR23's dates give 0.598, the value of independent days, and the lag-1 correlation of ∣rt​∣ falls from 0.161 (LM17) to about 0.

Resampling blocks of days keeps part of the clustering (LM22); volatility that depends on yesterday's is the subject of LM26.

PitfallResampling days is not a test on later data

The Research hygiene page says to split by time, never at random. A bootstrap draws days at random from the whole sample, mixing both limit regimes: 3,077 returns before 1 June 2015 and 2,772 from it. It shows how a statistic varies under the iid-days model; it is no test on later data (LM34). Reading a range of resamples as an interval for TAIEX is bootstrap inference, left to LM22.

導讀自助重抽法：保留單日分布，破壞群聚

自助重抽法（bootstrap）把經驗分布（empirical distribution）F^ 當成模型：重抽樣（resampling）是放回抽樣（sampling with replacement），每次以 1/T 的機率挑一天，所以一組重抽樣就是獨立同分布（iid）的抽樣。放回重抽樣（resampling with replacement）的平均數（mean），期望值（expectation）正好是 Rˉ、變異數（variance）正好是 s2/T，成長倍數（growth factor）的期望值是 (1+Rˉ)m。它保留了單日的分布，2025 年 4 月 7 日的 −9.70% 照樣可能被抽到；但它打亂了日期順序，波動的群聚（volatility clustering）完全消失：每月大波動日數的變異數從 1.846 掉到 0.598。所以自助重抽法量的是「各日獨立（independent）」這個模型下的變化，不是對未來資料的檢定。

Knowledge Check 6

What is the chance that 7 April 2025 is absent from a resample of 5,849 days, and what share of TR23's days appears in a resample on average?

Answer

Each of the 5,849 independent draws misses that day with probability 1−1/5,849, so by (13.7) it is absent with probability (1−1/5,849)5849=0.368. On average about 63% of the days appear, some several times.

8Simulation and Resampling in Python

implement reproducible simulations and bootstraps with NumPy's Generator and SciPy, in chunks

Exhibit 8 lists the NumPy and SciPy calls of this module, with the defaults that change results.

One generator per experiment, in chunks. Create the generator once, at the start of the experiment, and draw each path as a row, so that lnG is a row sum by (1.12). The code below is Example 3:

Python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

m, g, sr = 1231, 0.0005517, 0.012107           # sessions, rbar, s_r
rng = np.random.default_rng([3, 20261011])      # experiment 3, once
lnG = np.empty(10_000)
for c in range(0, 10_000, 500):                 # 20 chunks of 500 paths
    z = rng.standard_normal((500, m))
    lnG[c:c + 500] = (g + sr * z).sum(axis=1)   # ln G as a sum (1.12)
y = (lnG < 0).astype(float)
print(y.mean(), y.std() / np.sqrt(y.size))      # 0.053 0.00224...
print(stats.norm.cdf(-g * np.sqrt(m) / sr))     # 0.0549...

Chunks keep the memory small, and they double as the batches of a batch standard error.

PitfallAnother method draws other numbers

A seed fixes a stream of bits, not the draws of every method. From default_rng([2, 20261011]), norm.ppf(rng.random(3)) gives −1.0817, −0.0916 and −0.9382, while standard_normal(3) from a generator re-created with that seed gives 0.1679, 0.2891 and 0.7095. Likewise multivariate_normal gives other vectors than standard_normal((n, N)) @ L.T, because it factors the covariance matrix by SVD. Keep the method fixed when a result must reproduce.

In PythonCompanion lab

The Polars-first notebook LM18_lab.ipynb rebuilds the exhibits and computational examples from TR23's closes, with the seeds printed here. It solves the computational practice problems and ends by redoing the case under LM15's Student-t model.

The notebook reads FinMind files that you download once with your own token. From the repository root, run uv run python data/fetch_finmind.py, then uv run python data/make_lab_data.py. FinMind's licence does not allow the book to redistribute the data. After that, the notebook runs offline.

Knowledge Check 7

How much memory would 10,000 paths of 1,231 normal draws take at once, and why do chunks of 500 rows change no printed number?

Answer

At 8 bytes a float, 10,000×1,231 draws take 98.5 MB, and a chunk of 500 rows 4.9 MB. In the pinned NumPy, twenty calls of 500 rows consume the stream exactly as one call of 10,000 rows does, so every draw is the same. NumPy does not promise this, so data/lm18_numbers.py asserts it.

Summary

  • A seed reproduces every draw; another seed replicates the experiment.
  • The inverse transform (18.1) turns uniform draws into exponential, normal and empirical draws, and colouring gives normal vectors.
  • A Monte Carlo mean has standard error sY​/n​, (18.2), and a 95% Monte Carlo interval, (18.3), for simulation error only. LM12's gap of 0.0250 was an ordinary run of (18.4).
  • Quadrature wins in one dimension; in N dimensions a grid errs by O(n−4/N), Monte Carlo by O(n−1/2).
  • Antithetic variates (18.5), control variates (18.6) and importance sampling (18.7) keep the mean and cut the variance.
  • The iid bootstrap draws days from F^, with (18.8) and (18.9) exact. It agrees with the normal model on the case because both give lnG the same mean and variance.
  • Resampling keeps the one-day law and destroys the clustering.

Practice Problems

Problems on data use TR23: 5,849 daily returns, 3 January 2003 → 8 October 2026, moments with divisor T, A=246.12 and m=1,231.

  1. To divide a Monte Carlo standard error by 10 with the same method, multiply the number of draws by:

    • A.10
    • B.100
    • C.10​≈3.16

  2. Plain Monte Carlo estimates p=Pr(Z≤−3)=0.001350 from n=106 draws. The standard error of p^​ is closest to:

    • A.0.0367
    • B.1.35×10−9
    • C.3.67×10−5

  3. For U∼Unif(0,1), which is a draw from Exp(λ)?

    • A.−ln(1−U)/λ
    • B.−λln(1−U)
    • C.1−e−λU

  4. Five returns are +1.2%, −0.8%, +0.3%, −2.5% and +0.6%. Draw from their empirical distribution with u = 0.37, 0.95 and 0.18 by the rule R(⌈5u⌉)​. Why does u=0 give no draw?

  5. On the paths of Example 3, the plain estimates of EG and Pr(G<1) have standard errors 0.0097 and 0.0022. (a) Predict them for 5,000 antithetic pairs from (18.5), with ρ−​=−0.835 and −0.058. (b) Under the model, prove ρ−​=−e−mσr2​ for G and its partner e2mg/G, using (5.12).

  6. A control has ρXY​=0.95 with the simulated quantity. The number of plain draws that one controlled draw is worth is closest to:

    • A.1.11
    • B.10.3
    • C.20

  7. Derive the weight of (18.7) and, at a=k, the second moment ek2Φ(−2k) of one draw. For k=3, compare the variance of one draw with that of a plain draw.

  8. Prove VarF^​(Rˉboot​)=s2/T (divisor T), and evaluate its square root s/T​ with s=1.2084%. Does Example 9's 0.01563% reveal a flaw of the bootstrap?

  9. Apply (17.4) under F^ to obtain (18.9), and evaluate it with Rˉ=0.062505%. Compare it with emrˉ for rˉ=0.05517%.

  10. On a product grid in N dimensions Simpson's rule errs by O(n−4/N) and plain Monte Carlo by O(n−1/2). Monte Carlo has the better order when:

    • A.N>8
    • B.N>4
    • C.N>2

  11. Estimate the slope of Pr(Z≤−k) at k=2 by (2.11), with Δk=0.01 and 100,000 draws on each side. Given Φ(−2.01)=0.0222156 and Φ(−1.99)=0.0232955, find the exact central difference and its standard error with independent and with common draws.

  12. (Python) With a fresh default_rng([10, 20261011]), draw integers(0, T, size=(500, m)) twenty times and reproduce Example 10's PrF^​(Gboot​<1) and mean Gboot​ with their standard errors. Check that one call of size (10,000,m) gives identical indices.

Solutions

  1. B is correct. By (18.2) the standard error is sY​/n​, so dividing it by 10 needs n​ ten times larger, n a hundred times larger. A treats the error as 1/n, and C inverts the square root.

  2. C is correct. For an indicator σY2​=p(1−p), so the standard error is 0.001350×0.998650/106​=3.67×10−5. A, 0.0367, forgets n, and B, 1.35×10−9, is the variance of p^​, not its standard deviation.

  3. A is correct, by (18.1) with FY−1​(u)=−ln(1−u)/λ. B has mean λ instead of 1/λ: at λ=0.02992 its waits average 0.03 sessions instead of 33.4. C applies FY​ instead of FY−1​, and its values stay below 1−e−0.02992=0.0295.

  4. Sorted, the returns are −2.5%, −0.8%, +0.3%, +0.6% and +1.2%. The ranks are ⌈1.85⌉=2, ⌈4.75⌉=5 and ⌈0.9⌉=1, so the draws are −0.8%, +1.2% and −2.5%. For u=0, ⌈5×0⌉=0 is no rank: every x has F^(x)≥0, so the set in F^−1(0) has no minimum.

  5. (a) By (18.5), antithetic pairs multiply the variance by 1+ρ−​, so the standard error by 1+ρ−​​: 0.00971−0.835​=0.0039 for EG and 0.00221−0.058​=0.0021 for Pr(G<1), close to Example 6's results.

    (b) Under the model, lnG∼N(mg,mσr2​). The partner path has lnG−=2mg−lnG, so GG−=e2mg, and G− has the law of G. By (5.12), applied to lnG and to 2lnG,

    EGEG2Cov(G,G−)VarG​=EG−=emg+mσr2​/2,=e2mg+2mσr2​,=e2mg−(EG)2=−e2mg(emσr2​−1),=EG2−(EG)2=e2mg+mσr2​(emσr2​−1).​
    The ratio of the covariance to the variance is ρ−​=−e−mσr2​.

  6. B is correct. By (18.6) the variance falls by the factor 1−ρXY2​=1−0.952=0.0975, so one controlled draw is worth 1/0.0975=10.3 plain draws. A, 1.11, is 1/ρXY2​, and C, 20, is 1/(1−ρXY​), which forgets the square.

  7. Completing the square gives φ(z)eaz−a2/2=φ(z−a), so

    ​E[h(Z−a)eaZ−a2/2]=∫h(z−a)φ(z−a)dz=Eh(Z),​
    and the weight is eaZ−a2/2. Deep Dive (c) gives the second moment, ek2Φ(−2k) at a=k. For k=3, p=Φ(−3)=1.3499×10−3 and e9Φ(−6)=7.994×10−6, so one draw has variance 6.17×10−6. A plain draw has p(1−p)=1.348×10−3, 218 times as much.

  8. A day drawn from F^ has mean Rˉ and variance T1​∑t​(Rt​−Rˉ)2=s2. The T days of a resample are iid, so by (17.1) their mean has variance s2/T, and s/T​=1.2084%/5,849​=0.01580%. No: 0.01563% lies 1.5 of its standard errors, sY​/2B​=0.00011%, below the exact value, an ordinary simulation error.

  9. By (17.4), m independent days with mean μ give EWm​=W0​(1+μ)m. Under F^ the resampled days are independent with mean Rˉ, so EF^​Gboot​=(1+Rˉ)m, and 1.000625051231=2.1580. The median path is close to emrˉ=e1231×0.0005517=1.9722 by (17.6), lower than the mean path (LM17).

  10. A is correct. Monte Carlo's order n−1/2 beats n−4/N when 4/N<1/2, that is N>8. B uses the trapezoid rule's order n−2/N, and C a first-order rule.

  11. By (2.11) the exact central difference is (0.0222156−0.0232955)/0.02=−0.0540, equal to −φ(2) at this precision. With independent draws the variances of the two sides, 0.0222156×0.9777844 and 0.0232955×0.9767045, add up to 0.044475. With common draws the difference counts the draws in (−2.01,−1.99], an indicator with probability 0.0010799 and variance 0.0010799×0.9989201=0.0010787. The standard errors, independent and common, are

    0.020.044475/100,000​​=0.0333,0.020.0010787/100,000​​=0.0052.​

  12. With R TR23's daily simple returns as a NumPy array:

    Python
    import numpy as np

T, m = 5849, 1231
rng = np.random.default_rng([10, 20261011])          # experiment 10
idx = np.concatenate([rng.integers(0, T, size=(500, m))
                      for _ in range(20)])
G = np.prod(1 + R[idx], axis=1)                       # G_boot per row
y = (G < 1).astype(float)
print(y.mean(), y.std() / 100)                        # 0.0561 0.0023...
print(G.mean(), G.std() / 100)                        # 2.136... 0.0094...
one = np.random.default_rng([10, 20261011])
print((idx == one.integers(0, T, size=(10_000, m))).all())   # True

    The estimates are 0.0561±0.0023 and 2.136±0.009, against the exact 2.1580 of (18.9), and the comparison prints True in the pinned NumPy.

Glossary

Term 中文 Meaning
Pseudo-random number generator 擬隨機數產生器 A deterministic recursion whose outputs behave like iid uniform draws.
Seed 隨機種子 The number, or list of numbers, that sets a generator's starting state.
Common random numbers （兩次計算共用同一組隨機數） The same draws in two runs whose difference is wanted, so that their errors cancel.
Uniform distribution 均勻分布 Unif(0,1): Pr(U≤u)=u for 0≤u≤1.
Inverse transform 逆變換法 FY−1​(U) has distribution function FY​, (18.1).
Exponential distribution 指數分布 Exp(λ): FY​(y)=1−e−λy, mean 1/λ, median ln2/λ.
Monte Carlo estimator 蒙地卡羅估計量 The mean Yˉn​ of n iid draws, an estimate of EY, (18.2).
Standard error 標準誤 sY​/n​, the estimated standard deviation of Yˉn​.
95% Monte Carlo interval （只量模擬誤差的區間） Yˉn​±1.96sY​/n​, (18.3); it measures simulation error only.
Frobenius norm Frobenius 範數 ∥M∥F​, the square root of the sum of the squared entries.
Variance reduction 變異數縮減 A change of what is averaged that keeps the expectation and lowers the variance.
Antithetic variates 對偶變數 Pairs of draws from Z and −Z, (18.5).
Control variate 控制變量 A quantity with known mean that corrects the estimate, (18.6).
Importance sampling 重要抽樣 Drawing from a shifted law and weighting the draws back, (18.7).
Bootstrap 自助重抽法 Treating the empirical distribution F^ as the model and drawing from it.
Resampling with replacement 放回重抽樣 Drawing days from the sample, each with probability 1/T at every draw.
